```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, fig.align = "center")
options(scipen = 999)

# Install these packages once using install.packages() if necessary.
needed <- c("haven", "dplyr", "knitr")
missing_packages <- needed[!vapply(needed, requireNamespace,
                                    logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  stop("Install these R packages before knitting: ",
       paste(missing_packages, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
}
library(dplyr)

# Place the OFFICIAL file in a 'data' folder beside this Rmd.
# Source: https://www.openicpsr.org/openicpsr/project/113224/version/V1/view
file <- file.path("data", "AERtables1-5.dta")
if (!file.exists(file)) {
  stop("Official data file not found: ", file,
       "\nDownload AERtables1-5.dta from openICPSR study 113224 and ",
       "place it in the data/ folder next to this Rmd.", call. = FALSE)
}

raw_data <- haven::read_dta(file)
required <- c("treatment", "control", "ratio", "gave", "amount",
              "ratio2", "ratio3", "size25", "size50", "size100",
              "askd2", "askd3")
absent <- setdiff(required, names(raw_data))
if (length(absent) > 0) {
  stop("Variables not found in the official dataset: ",
       paste(absent, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
}

# Keep observations with complete experimental assignment and outcomes.
# The published tables use 50,083 people. The released file can contain
# additional rows with missing experiment fields. We do not impute them.
data <- raw_data |>
  filter(if_all(all_of(required), ~ !is.na(.x))) |>
  filter(treatment %in% c(0, 1), control %in% c(0, 1),
         treatment + control == 1,
         gave %in% c(0, 1), ratio %in% c(0, 1, 2, 3))

# A mismatch is a substantive issue; do not force a published sample size.
if (nrow(data) != 50083 || sum(data$treatment == 1) != 33396 ||
    sum(data$control == 1) != 16687) {
  stop("Analysis sample does not match the published allocation (50,083; ",
       "33,396 treatment; 16,687 control). Check the official files ",
       "and the original Stata script before using the estimates. ",
       "Current sample: ", nrow(data), call. = FALSE)
}

fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
fmt_se <- function(x, se) sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", x, se)
```

# Introduction

Does offering to match a charitable donation encourage people to give? Moreover, if a match is effective, does a more generous match attract larger donations? Karlan and List (2007) examine these questions using a natural field experiment conducted with a US nonprofit organization. Their study appears in the *American Economic Review*.

This report reproduces a small selection of their main findings. Rather than repeating every analysis, it concentrates on whether matching grants affect the decision to donate, the average amount contributed, and the response to different matching ratios. The aim is to show the empirical results clearly and examine what they imply.

# Experimental design and data

The researchers sent fundraising letters to 50,083 previous donors. Among them, 16,687 received a standard letter (control group), while 33,396 were offered a matching grant (treatment group). This meant that an external donor would add money to their donation. For example, under a 1:1 ratio, every \$1 donated would be matched with an additional \$1. Under a 2:1 or 3:1 ratio, the external donor would contribute \$2 or \$3 for every \$1 donated. The researchers randomly assigned these different ratios to examine whether more generous matching offers encouraged people to give more. They also varied the maximum amount that could be matched and the suggested donation amount included in the letter.

I use the authors' public data file, `AERtables1-5.dta`, from the [openICPSR replication archive](https://www.openicpsr.org/openicpsr/project/113224/version/V1/view) (study 113224, version V1).

The main outcomes are `gave`, an indicator for whether a person contributed, and `amount`, the dollars personally given by the recipient of the letter. The latter includes zeros for individuals who did not donate, and excludes the matching donor's additional contribution. Therefore, an increase in `amount` reflects additional giving by solicited individuals rather than the mechanical value of the grant.

```{r data-check}
# A compact verification of the randomized groups.
data |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(Observations = n(),
            `Response rate` = mean(gave),
            `Dollars per letter` = mean(amount),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Treatment (1 = match)", "Observations",
                             "Response rate", "Dollars per letter"),
               caption = "Analysis sample, computed from the official dataset.")
```

# Empirical approach

Because the matching offer was assigned at random, the difference between treatment and control means identifies the intention-to-treat effect of receiving an offer. In particular, I estimate the simple linear regression

$$Y_i = \alpha + \beta\,\text{Treatment}_i + \varepsilon_i.$$

Here, $Y_i$ is either an indicator for giving or the amount donated, and $\beta$ is the average treatment–control difference. For the binary outcome, I also fit a Probit model and calculate the discrete change in predicted probability between treatment and control.

To study matching ratios, I follow the structure of the richer specification in Table 4 of the article. The model includes the treatment indicator, separate indicators for the 2:1 and 3:1 ratios, and the other randomized features of the matching offer. Hence, the two ratio coefficients compare 2:1 and 3:1 with the omitted 1:1 group, rather than with the control group.

# Replication results

## 1. Donation decisions and donation amounts

First, I compare the mean outcomes across the experimental groups. The table below corresponds to the principal descriptive results in *Table 2A, Panel A* of Karlan and List (2007). The full treatment column pools all three match ratios, whereas the ratio columns refer only to the corresponding treatment arms.

```{r descriptive-results}
# Three disjoint match groups plus the pooled treatment group.
groups <- list(
  "Control" = data |> filter(treatment == 0),
  "Any match" = data |> filter(treatment == 1),
  "Match 1:1" = data |> filter(treatment == 1, ratio == 1),
  "Match 2:1" = data |> filter(treatment == 1, ratio == 2),
  "Match 3:1" = data |> filter(treatment == 1, ratio == 3)
)

rep_descriptive <- data.frame(
  Group = names(groups),
  N = vapply(groups, nrow, integer(1)),
  `Response rate` = vapply(groups, function(x) mean(x$gave), numeric(1)),
  `Dollars per letter` = vapply(groups, function(x) mean(x$amount), numeric(1)),
  `Dollars among donors` = vapply(groups,
     function(x) mean(x$amount[x$gave == 1]), numeric(1)),
  check.names = FALSE
)

published_descriptive <- data.frame(
  Group = c("Control", "Any match", "Match 1:1", "Match 2:1", "Match 3:1"),
  N = c(16687, 33396, 11133, 11134, 11129),
  `Response rate` = c(.018, .022, .021, .023, .023),
  `Dollars per letter` = c(.813, .967, .937, 1.026, .938),
  `Dollars among donors` = c(45.540, 43.872, 45.143, 45.337, 41.252),
  check.names = FALSE
)

show_desc <- rep_descriptive
for (v in c("Response rate", "Dollars per letter", "Dollars among donors")) {
  show_desc[[v]] <- fmt(show_desc[[v]])
}
knitr::kable(show_desc,
  caption = "Table 1. Replicated descriptive outcomes (author's calculations).",
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"))

```

The published results show a response rate of 1.8% in the control group and 2.2% among recipients of a matching offer. This corresponds to an increase of approximately 0.4 percentage points, or around 22% relative to the control rate. Likewise, the average personal donation per letter rises from \$0.813 to \$0.967. Although these differences are small in absolute terms, they matter in a fundraising campaign involving many recipients.

In contrast, the mean donation among people who donated is lower in the treatment group. This conditional difference does not identify a causal effect on gift size, because the offer can also change who decides to give.

## 2. Effects of offering a matching grant

I now estimate the treatment effect directly. The first estimate uses a Probit model for the probability of donating. The second uses ordinary least squares (OLS) for the dollar amount donated, including zeros. They are compared with *Table 3, column 1* and *Table 4, Panel A, column 1* of the paper.

```{r main-regressions}
# Probit: compute the change in predicted probability from 0 to 1.
probit <- glm(gave ~ treatment, data = data,
              family = binomial(link = "probit"))
a <- unname(coef(probit)["(Intercept)"])
b <- unname(coef(probit)["treatment"])
probability_effect <- pnorm(a + b) - pnorm(a)

# Delta-method SE for the discrete change in predicted probability.
# The published Stata calculation may use a different marginal-effect
# convention, so compare the results rather than assuming identity.
gradient <- c(dnorm(a + b) - dnorm(a), dnorm(a + b))
probability_se <- sqrt(as.numeric(t(gradient) %*%
                   vcov(probit) %*% gradient))

# OLS: unconditional donation amount (including zero donations).
ols_amount <- lm(amount ~ treatment, data = data)
ols_amount_est <- unname(coef(ols_amount)["treatment"])
ols_amount_se <- summary(ols_amount)$coefficients["treatment", "Std. Error"]

main_table <- data.frame(
  Outcome = c("Probability of giving — Probit difference",
              "Dollars given per letter — OLS"),
  `Published estimate (SE)` = c("0.004 (0.001)", "0.154 (0.083)"),
  `Reproduced estimate (SE)` = c(
    fmt_se(probability_effect, probability_se),
    fmt_se(ols_amount_est, ols_amount_se)),
  N = c(nobs(probit), nobs(ols_amount)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(main_table, caption = paste(
  "Table 2. Matching-offer effects. Published values: Table 3 (1) and",
  "Table 4, Panel A (1). Probit estimate is a discrete probability difference."))
```

The key distinction is between the extensive margin (whether someone gives at all) and the unconditional amount donated (which combines the decision to give and the amount given). Random assignment allows the estimated difference for these outcomes to be interpreted causally as the effect of receiving the matching offer in this experiment.

For the dollar outcome, the simple OLS treatment coefficient is also the difference in mean donations. Statistical uncertainty is important: a small positive estimate need not imply that every recipient increases their contribution.

## 3. Does a more generous match work better?

Finally, I examine whether the 2:1 and 3:1 offers outperform the 1:1 offer. To make the comparison consistent with *Table 4, Panel A, column 2*, I retain the authors' additional randomized treatment dimensions: stated match ceilings and suggested donation examples. The omitted categories are the 1:1 ratio, no stated ceiling, and the low suggested amount.

```{r ratio-regression}
# The published specification uses these supplied treatment indicators.
# There are no extra hand-built variables, interactions, or external scripts.
ratio_model <- lm(
  amount ~ treatment + ratio2 + ratio3 +
    size25 + size50 + size100 + askd2 + askd3,
  data = data
)

coef_table <- summary(ratio_model)$coefficients
chosen <- c("treatment", "ratio2", "ratio3")
ratio_table <- data.frame(
  Comparison = c("1:1 offer vs control (reference offer)",
                 "Extra effect: 2:1 vs 1:1",
                 "Extra effect: 3:1 vs 1:1"),
  `Published estimate (SE)` = c("0.118 (0.151)",
                                "0.089 (0.117)",
                                "0.001 (0.117)"),
  `Reproduced estimate (SE)` = vapply(chosen, function(v) {
    fmt_se(coef_table[v, "Estimate"], coef_table[v, "Std. Error"])
  }, character(1)),
  N = rep(nobs(ratio_model), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(ratio_table,
             caption = "Table 3. Treatment and ratio comparisons; published benchmark: Table 4, Panel A (2).")
```

Recall that a 2:1 offer means that a matching donor contributes \$2 for every \$1 given by the recipient; for 3:1, the matching donor contributes \$3. The relevant comparisons are the additional coefficients on `ratio2` and `ratio3`. Neither coefficient in the published regression is statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional levels. Thus, the evidence supports a distinction between offering a match and increasing the match ratio: the former appears to encourage donations, while the latter does not produce a clearly measurable additional gain in personal donations.

Importantly, this is not evidence that the true differences must be exactly zero. The estimates are subject to sampling uncertainty.

# Discussion and limitations

Taken together, these results suggest that the announcement of a matching grant can stimulate charitable giving. However, a more generous match does not necessarily generate higher participation or personal contributions. For fundraising organizations, the design of a matching campaign may therefore matter as much as its nominal generosity.

This is a deliberately selective replication. It focuses on the full experimental sample and the two primary outcomes, rather than reproducing the authors' geographical analyses or every model. The study involved previous donors to one politically oriented US nonprofit in 2005, so the effect need not generalize to first-time donors, other organizations, or other periods.

There is also a methodological distinction: the Probit probability contrast above is a discrete change in fitted probabilities, with a delta-method standard error. Older Stata commands can report marginal effects using a different convention. Any difference from the published Probit coefficient should be assessed in that light. The OLS regressions use conventional model-based standard errors, as in the simple published columns; alternative heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors could change precision without changing the estimated coefficients.

# Conclusion

This replication studies two closely related questions: whether matching offers encourage charitable giving and whether more generous matching ratios are more effective. The published evidence indicates that matching offers increase participation and average donations per mailing, while raising the match ratio beyond 1:1 does not yield a clear additional increase. Re-estimating the selected results in R provides a compact example of causal inference from randomized field-experiment data.

# References and replication materials

Karlan, Dean, and John A. List. 2007. “Does Price Matter in Charitable Giving? Evidence from a Large-Scale Natural Field Experiment.” *American Economic Review* 97 (5): 1774–1793. <https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.5.1774>.

Karlan, Dean, and John A. List. 2019. *Replication data for: Does Price Matter in Charitable Giving? Evidence from a Large-Scale Natural Field Experiment.* openICPSR, version V1. <https://doi.org/10.3886/E113224V1>.

Original authors' analysis file: `AERtables1-5.do`, archived alongside `AERtables1-5.dta` at openICPSR. The published benchmark values in Tables 1–3 of this report are transcribed from the article; the reproduced columns and differences are calculated by the code above.
